question: Fold a piece of paper and unfold it. Do you see a crease? (This gives the idea of a line segment. It has two end points, A and B.)
answer: Yes, the crease is a straight mark; it gives the idea of a line segment with two end points A and B.
steps: Fold the paper and open it.
The crease is straight and has two ends: A and B.
figure: Rectangle of paper with a straight crease from A (top edge) to B (bottom edge).
note: Book states the idea in the text; no printed solution.

question: Mark any two points A and B on a sheet of paper. Try to connect A to B by various routes (Fig. 2.1). What is the shortest route from A to B?
answer: The straight path from A to B, which is the line segment AB.
steps: Draw several routes from A to B (zig-zag, curved).
Compare lengths; the straight route is shortest.
This shortest path including A and B is the line segment AB.
figure: Fig. 2.1: A and B joined by several wiggly routes with arrowheads and one straight line.
note: The book gives the answer in the following sentence of the text; no solution-page entry.

question: Imagine that the line segment AB is extended beyond A in one direction and beyond B in the other direction without any end (Fig. 2.2). Do you think you can draw a complete picture of a line? No. Why?
answer: No, because a line goes on forever in both directions, so only a part of it can be drawn (arrowheads show it continues).
steps: A line has no end in either direction.
Paper is finite, so we can draw only a part and put arrows at both ends.
figure: Fig. 2.2: line m with arrows at both ends, points A and B on it.
note: Book prints 'No. Why?' and then states that a line extends forever in both directions; no solution-page entry.

question: Rihan marked a point on a piece of paper. How many lines can he draw that pass through the point? Sheetal marked two points on a piece of paper. How many different lines can she draw that pass through both of the points? Can you help Rihan and Sheetal find their answers?

parts.label: Rihan
parts.question: How many lines can be drawn through one marked point?

parts.label: Sheetal
parts.question: How many different lines through both of two marked points?

answer: Rihan: many (uncountably many) lines. Sheetal: only one line.
steps: Through one point, lines can point in any direction, so there are endlessly many.
Two points determine a unique line.
figure: Two speech boxes only.

book_label: 2.4 Ray, Figure it Out Q2, Fig. 2.4 (page 16)
question: Name the line segments in Fig. 2.4. Which of the five marked points are on exactly one of the line segments? Which are on two of the line segments? (Fig. 2.4 is a zig-zag path L-M-P-Q-R: L to M, M to P, P to Q, Q to R.)
answer: Segments LM, MP, PQ, QR. L and R are on exactly one segment; M, P and Q are on two segments.
steps: Each straight piece between consecutive marked points is a segment.
End points L and R belong to one piece each.
M, P, Q are joints shared by two pieces.
figure: Zig-zag path L-M-P-Q-R with five marked points; segments LM, MP, PQ, QR.

book_label: 2.4 Ray, Figure it Out Q3, Fig. 2.5 (page 16)
question: Name the rays shown in Fig. 2.5. Is T the starting point of each of these rays? (Fig. 2.5: from T one ray goes up-right through A; another goes right through N and then B.)

parts.label: b
parts.question: Is T the starting point of each?
parts.answer: No. T is the starting point of TB, TN and TA but not of NB.

answer: Rays TA, TB, TN and NB. No: T is the starting point of TA, TB and TN, but not of NB (which starts at N).
steps: Ray TA starts at T through A.
On the horizontal ray, TN and TB start at T; NB starts at N and goes through B.
figure: Fig. 2.5: T at the left; ray through A going up-right; horizontal ray through N then B with arrowhead.
note: The printed solution lists the rays as TA, TB, TN and NB; the arrow marks over the letters are rendered in the solutions page as plain right arrows.

question: Draw a rough figure and write labels appropriately to illustrate each of the following: a. OP and OQ (lines) meet at O. b. XY (ray) and PQ (line) intersect at point M. c. Line l contains points E and F but not point D. d. Point P lies on AB.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Line OP and line OQ meet at O.
parts.answer: Draw two lines crossing at O, one through P and one through Q.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Ray XY and line PQ intersect at point M.
parts.answer: Draw ray XY from X through Y and line PQ crossing it at M.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Line l contains E and F but not D.
parts.answer: Draw line l through E and F with D marked away from the line.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Point P lies on AB.
parts.answer: Mark P on the segment between A and B.

answer: Drawings: (a) two double-arrow lines crossing at O with P and Q on them; (b) ray XY and line PQ crossing at M; (c) line l through E and F with D off the line; (d) P between A and B on the segment AB.
steps: Draw each figure with the stated labels.
note: Book's solutions show drawings: (a) two crossing lines (one through P, one through Q, crossing at O), (b) ray XY from X through M to Y and line PQ through M, (c) line l with E and F, D below, (d) segment A-P-B. In the problem, OP and OQ are written with double arrows (lines); XY has a single arrow (ray); AB in part d is printed with a bar in the solutions.

book_label: 2.4 Ray, Figure it Out Q5, Fig. 2.6 (page 16)
question: In Fig. 2.6, name: a. Five points b. A line c. Four rays d. Five line segments. (Fig. 2.6: a line passes through D, E, O, B; a ray from O goes through C; another ray from O goes straight up.)

parts.label: a
parts.question: Five points
parts.answer: D, E, O, B and C

parts.label: b
parts.question: A line
parts.answer: DE or DO or DB or EO or EB or OB (any two of the points D, E, O, B, written with a double arrow)

parts.label: c
parts.question: Four rays
parts.answer: OC, OB, OE, OD (other rays are possible)

parts.label: d
parts.question: Five line segments
parts.answer: DE, DO, DB, EO, EB (OB and OC are also possible)

answer: a) D, E, O, B, C. b) the line through D, E, O, B, e.g. line DB. c) rays OC, OB, OE, OD. d) segments DE, DO, DB, EO, EB.
steps: Collect the marked points.
Any two of D, E, O, B name the line.
Rays start at O or E etc. and pass through another point.
Segments are pieces between two marked points.
figure: Line with points D (lower left), E, O, B (upper right) in that order; ray from O through C going right; an extra ray from O going straight up with no marked point.

book_label: 2.4 Ray, Figure it Out Q6, Fig. 2.7 (page 17)
question: Here is a ray OA (Fig. 2.7). It starts at O and passes through the point A. It also passes through the point B. a. Can you also name it as OB? Why? b. Can we write OA as AO? Why or why not?

parts.label: a
parts.question: Can you also name it as OB? Why?
parts.answer: Yes. O is the starting point and B lies on the ray that goes endlessly in the direction of A, so OA is the same ray as OB.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Can we write OA as AO? Why or why not?
parts.answer: No. OA is a ray with starting point O, whereas AO is a ray with starting point A.

answer: a) Yes, the ray starts at O and B is on it. b) No, AO would start at A.
steps: A ray is named by its starting point first, then any other point on it.
OA and OB start at O and go the same way, so they are the same ray.
AO starts at A, so it is a different ray.
figure: Fig. 2.7: ray from O going up-right through B (nearer) and A (further), arrowhead at the far end.

question: Vidya opens the cover of her book in six cases (Case 1 to Case 6). Do you see angles being made in each of these cases? Can you mark their arms and vertex?
answer: Yes, an angle is formed in each case. The arms are the cover and the rest of the book (the two rays along the cover and the book); the vertex is the hinge/spine where they meet.
steps: The book cover and the page below it form the two arms.
The vertex is the hinge where they join.
figure: Six pictures of Vidya opening a book cover, Case 1 slightly open up to Case 6 widest.
note: No printed solution; the vertex/arms description is computed from the pictures.

question: Which angle is greater: the angle in Case 1 or the angle in Case 2?
answer: The angle in Case 2 is greater, because she needs to rotate the cover more.
steps: The size of an angle is the amount of rotation.
In Case 2 the cover is rotated more than in Case 1.
figure: Cases 1 and 2: Case 2 has the cover opened wider than Case 1.
note: Answer is stated in the book text right after the question (Case 2 is greater; Case 3 larger than Case 2; Cases 4, 5, 6 successively larger).

question: In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle. The vertex is the point where the two arms are joined. Identify the arms and vertex of the angle.
answer: The two legs of the compass are the arms; the vertex is the joint (hinge) at the top where the arms are joined.
steps: The two legs are the arms.
The joint where they meet is the vertex.
figure: Picture of a compass (divider) with a pencil.
note: Computed from the text and picture.

question: A pair of scissors has two blades. When we open them (or 'turn them') to cut something, the blades form an angle. Identify the arms and the vertex of the angle.
answer: The two blades are the arms; the vertex is the screw/pivot where the blades are joined.
steps: The blades are the arms.
The pivot screw is the vertex.
figure: Picture of open scissors with purple handles.
note: Computed from the text and picture.

book_label: 2.5 Angle, spectacles, wallet and other objects (page 19)
question: Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common objects (a stapler, a hinged box, a box with an open flap). Identify the angles in them by marking out their arms and vertices.
answer: Each object has two parts joined at a hinge; the two parts are the arms and the hinge is the vertex (e.g., spectacles: a temple (side arm) and the frame; wallet: the two halves; stapler: the top and base; box: lid and box).
steps: Find the two parts that turn about a hinge.
Those parts are the arms; the hinge is the vertex.
figure: Five pictures: spectacles, an open wallet, a stapler, a hinged box (tin) slightly open, a cardboard box with an open flap.
note: No printed solution.

question: Do you see how these angles are formed by turning one arm with respect to the other?
answer: Yes. Each angle is formed when one arm is turned about the vertex relative to the other.
steps: One arm stays, the other turns about the vertex.
The amount of turn is the size of the angle.
note: Reflective question; no printed answer.

question: Can you find the angles in the given pictures? Draw the rays forming any one of the angles and name the vertex of the angle. (Pictures: a bicycle with points A, B, C, D and arrows marked on it, a wooden crate with slanting slats, a ladder, a bridge.)
answer: Yes. For example, in the bicycle one angle is ∠BDC with vertex D; one ray is DC and the other ray is DB. Try for other pictures.
steps: Pick two lines or parts meeting at a point.
Draw them as rays from that point and name the vertex.
figure: Bicycle with arrows: points A (front wheel centre), B (seat tube area), C (handle), D (pedal/crank); crate with slats; ladder; truss bridge.
note: The book's sample answer uses angle BDC from the bicycle picture; the labelled points on the printed bicycle are small and hard to read (A, B, C, D visible). Pictures continue on page 20 (ladder, bridge).

question: Draw and label an angle with arms ST and SR.
answer: Draw two rays from S: one through T and one through R, with a curve at S. The angle is ∠RST (or ∠TSR) with vertex S.
steps: Mark the vertex S.
Draw ray ST and ray SR from S.
Mark a small curve between them.
figure: Solution drawing: vertex S at bottom left, horizontal ray to T, ray going up-right to R, with a small curve at S.
note: The book's solution drawing is shown (R above, T on the right). On the solutions page the drawing sits under Q2 but its label text 'Ans.' is followed directly by Q4 text.

question: Explain why ∠APB cannot be labelled as ∠P. (Figure: vertex P with three rays going through A (upper), B (middle) and C (lower).)
answer: Three angles share the vertex P (∠APB, ∠BPC and ∠APC). Naming one as ∠P would not say which of them is meant, so we must name a point on each arm.
steps: At P there are three rays, PA, PB, PC.
So there are three different angles at P.
∠P alone cannot tell which one; use points on both arms.
figure: Vertex P with rays through A (up-right), B (right, horizontal), C (down-right).
note: No solution printed for Q3 in the book's solutions (skips Q3). A Math Talk marker is beside this figure.

question: Name the angles marked in the given figure. (Figure: vertex T with rays to P, Q and R; curved marks drawn at T.)
answer: ∠RTQ and ∠RTP (as printed in the book's solutions).
steps: Read the marked curves at T.
Name each angle with T in the middle.
figure: Vertex T; ray TR horizontal to the right, ray TQ up (steeper than 45 degrees, slightly right), ray TP steep up-left of Q. Curved marks at T near TP-TQ and TQ-TR.
note: UNSURE: the solution page prints '∠RTQ, ∠RTP' but the drawing above it is the S, T, R figure from Q2, not this P, Q, R, T figure. In the question's figure the arcs appear to mark angle PTQ (small arc) and an arc across TQ-TR; the printed answer names ∠RTQ and ∠RTP. Use the printed answer; verify against the picture.

question: Mark any three points on your paper that are not on one line. Label them A, B, C. Draw all possible lines going through pairs of these points. How many lines do you get? Name them. How many angles can you name using A, B, C? Write them down, and mark each of them with a curve as in Fig. 2.9.

parts.label: angles
parts.question: How many angles using A, B, C?

answer: Three lines AB, BC, CA and three angles ∠ABC, ∠BCA, ∠CAB.
steps: Join each pair of points: AB, BC, CA gives 3 lines.
Each point is a vertex of one angle, giving 3 angles.
figure: Solution drawing: triangle ABC with all three lines extended and a curve marked at each of A, B, C.

question: Now mark any four points on your paper so that no three of them are on one line. Label them A, B, C, D. Draw all possible lines going through pairs of these points. How many lines do you get? Name them. How many angles can you name using A, B, C, D? Write them all down, and mark each of them with a curve as in Fig. 2.9.

parts.label: lines
parts.question: How many lines? Name them.
parts.answer: 6 lines: AB, BC, CD, DA, AC, BD

parts.label: angles
parts.question: How many angles using A, B, C, D?

answer: Six lines AB, BC, CD, DA, AC, BD and twelve angles: ∠BAC, ∠CAD, ∠BAD, ∠ADB, ∠BDC, ∠ADC, ∠DCA, ∠ACB, ∠DCB, ∠CBD, ∠DBA, ∠CBA.
steps: Pairs of 4 points: 6 lines.
At each point the other three points give 3 angles; 4 points × 3 = 12 angles.
figure: Solution drawing: four points A, B, C, D with all six lines drawn, curves at each vertex.
note: The 'at each point 3 angles' step is added by me (computed); the 12 names are exactly as printed (the book writes ∠CBA and ∠DBA last).

question: Look at these animals opening their mouths (snake, fish, bird, crocodile). Do you see any angles here? If yes, mark the arms and vertex of each one. Some mouths are open wider than others; the more the turning of the jaws, the larger the angle! Can you arrange the angles in this picture from smallest to largest?
answer: Yes, each mouth makes an angle (the two jaws are the arms; the hinge of the jaws is the vertex). Arrange them by how wide each mouth is open; the crocodile's looks widest.
steps: Mark the jaws as arms and the hinge as the vertex.
Compare the amounts of opening and order them.
figure: Four animal pictures: snake (mouth moderately open), fish (mouth slightly open), bird in nest (mouth small), crocodile (mouth wide open).
note: No printed order. The crocodile looks widest and the fish narrowest in the picture, but the book gives no answer.

question: Is it always easy to compare two angles?
answer: No. It is not always easy to compare two angles; for example angles of 89 degrees and 91 degrees cannot be compared without measuring or overlapping. For the given figures, comparison is easy.
steps: Angles with nearly the same opening look alike.
We need superimposition (or measuring) to be sure.
note: Solution page 'Page 20'.

book_label: 2.6 Comparing Angles, page 21 (four drawn angles, Math Talk)
question: Here are some angles (four angles drawn with different openings and orientations). Label each of the angles. How will you compare them? Draw a few more angles; label them and compare.
answer: Label each angle (e.g., ∠1 to ∠4 with letters), then compare them by superimposition: place vertices together and one arm over another to see which is larger.
steps: Label the vertex and one point on each arm.
Compare by superimposing pairs of angles.
figure: Four angles marked with small curves at their vertices: 1 (near-vertical arm, medium opening), 2 (arms up-right and down, larger), 3 (small opening at the right with arms pointing left and down-left), 4 (vertex at lower right, arms going up-left and left, larger).
note: No printed answer. Math Talk marker is beside the figure.

book_label: 2.6 Comparing angles by superimposition, equal angles (page 22)
question: Now consider ∠AOB and ∠XOY in the figure. Which is greater?
answer: Neither. The angles are equal in size, because when superimposed the vertex O and the arms OA with OX and OB with OY lie on top of each other.
steps: Superimpose the angles with O on O.
Arm OA falls on OX and OB falls on OY.
So the two angles are equal.
figure: ∠AOB and ∠XOY drawn with the same opening; superimposed copy shows arms overlapping (B and Y on the same base ray).
note: Answer stated in the book text after the question.

question: Where else do we use superimposition to compare?
answer: A few examples are line segments, squares and circles. Think of more.
steps: Place one shape over another to compare size.
note: Open-ended beyond the examples listed in the solutions.

book_label: 2.6 Comparing Angles, Figure it Out Q1 (page 23)
question: Fold a rectangular sheet of paper, then draw a line along the fold created. Name and compare the angles formed between the fold and the sides of the paper. Make different angles by folding a rectangular sheet of paper and compare the angles. Which is the largest and smallest angle you made?
answer: Example from the book: a slanting crease EF from E on one long side to F on the opposite side gives the angles ∠AEF, ∠BEF, ∠DFE, ∠CFE. ∠AEF and ∠CFE are larger than ∠BEF and ∠DFE. Try more cases; the largest and smallest depend on the folds you make.
steps: Fold the sheet and mark the crease.
Name the four angles between the crease and the sides.
Compare by superimposition or folding.
figure: Rectangle with slanting fold line EF; ABCD rectangle with A and B at bottom right/left, C and D top left/right; angles marked at E and F.
note: Largest/smallest depends on the child's own folds (open-ended part). In the solution figure, B and A are the bottom corners (B left, A right) and C, D the top corners (C left, D right).

book_label: 2.6 Comparing Angles, Figure it Out Q2 (page 23)
question: In each case, determine which angle is greater and why. a. ∠AOB or ∠XOY b. ∠AOB or ∠XOB c. ∠XOB or ∠XOC. Discuss with your friends on how you decided which one is greater. (Figure: O is the vertex; OA is vertical, OX and OY are slanting rays with OX steeper, B and C are on the same horizontal ray, B nearer O.)
answer: a) ∠AOB b) ∠AOB c) neither; they are equal.
steps: a) ∠AOB contains ∠XOY inside it, so it is greater.
b) ∠XOB lies inside ∠AOB.
c) B and C lie on the same ray from O, so the arms are the same.
figure: Vertex O; ray OA vertical up; ray OX steep up-right; ray OY shallower up-right; ray along the horizontal through B (near) then C (far). Rays OX and OY lie between OA and OB.
note: The printed solution for (a) literally reads '∠AOB; ∠XOY is an acute angle and ∠AOB = ∠AOX + ∠XOY + ∠YOB' - kept verbatim; ∠AOB looks like a right angle in the picture. Math Talk marker is beside the figure.

book_label: 2.6 Comparing Angles, Figure it Out Q3 (page 23)
question: Which angle is greater: ∠XOY or ∠AOB? Give reasons. (Figure: vertex O; OX up-left, OA up-right, OY nearly horizontal slightly up, OB horizontal.)
answer: By looking at the figure we cannot say. Superimposition or measurement is necessary here.
steps: The two angles are oriented differently and look close in size.
Superimpose them (vertices together, one arm over another) to decide.
figure: Vertex O with four rays: OX up-left, OA up-right and steep, OY slightly above horizontal, OB horizontal.

book_label: 2.6 Comparing angles without superimposition, transparent circle (page 24)
question: A transparent circle is placed on the angle of the first crane with its centre at the vertex; A and B are marked where the arms cross the circle. The circle is then placed on the second crane's angle with the vertex at the centre and one arm through OA. Can you now tell which angle is bigger?
answer: Compare where the second arm meets the circle (point Y) with B. If the second arm passes beyond B the second angle is bigger; if it lands on B they are equal; if short of B, smaller. In the picture Y is beyond/near B, so compare the positions on the circle (the arc between the points decides).
steps: Match one arm of each angle with OA.
Compare the other end points on the circle (B and Y).
A farther end point means a bigger angle.
figure: Transparent circle with centre O on the second crane's angle; arm through A (also marked X); other arm through Y, which is close to B (B marked slightly left of Y).
note: UNSURE: no printed answer. In the picture, B and Y are very close (Y slightly right of B on the circle); the book then asks 'Which crane was making the bigger angle?' on the next page without answering. Do not treat the answer as fixed.

question: Which crane was making the bigger angle? If you can make a circular piece of transparent paper, try this method to compare the angles in Fig. 2.10 with each other.
answer: Trace both beak angles, place the transparent circle centred on the vertex, mark where the arms cross the circle, and compare the gaps between the marked points; the crane whose arms are farther apart (right crane in the picture) makes the bigger angle.
steps: Place the circle's centre on the vertex of each crane's angle.
Mark A and B where the arms cross the circle.
Slide the circle to the other angle, keep one arm on OA, and compare where the other arm crosses.
figure: Fig. 2.10: two cranes with open beaks; the right crane's beak looks wider than the left one's.
note: UNSURE: no printed answer. 'Right crane wider' is my reading of the picture, not printed.

question: Make several 'rotating arms' (two paper straws and a paper clip) with different angles between the arms. Arrange the angles you have made from smallest to largest by comparing and using superimposition.
answer: Place the arms over each other with the joints together and compare the openings; arrange them in order.
steps: Take two paper straws and a paper clip.
Insert the straws into the arms of the paper clip.
Set different angles and compare by superimposing.
Arrange from smallest to largest.
figure: Three pictures: straws and clip; straws pushed into the clip; finished V-shaped rotating arm.
note: Hands-on activity.

question: Collect a number of rotating arms with different angles (do not rotate any of them). Take a cardboard and make an angle-shaped slit by tracing and cutting out the shape of one of the rotating arms. Now shuffle and mix up all the rotating arms. Can you identify which of the rotating arms will pass through the slit?
answer: Only the arm whose angle is equal to the slit's angle passes through; place each over the slit to find it. Passing through depends only on the angle, not on the arms' lengths (as long as they are shorter than the slit).
steps: Place an arm over the slit.
If the slit angle is greater than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
If the slit angle is less than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
If equal, the arms go through.
figure: Three cardboard slits: slit angle greater than arms' angle (does not pass), less than arms' angle (does not pass), equal (passes).
note: The rule is printed in the book text.

question: Challenge: Reduce this angle. (A girl snips the ends of the arms of a V-shaped rotating arm with scissors: 'Angle reduced.' The boy says 'The angle is still the same!')
answer: Cutting the arms shorter does not change the angle; the size of an angle depends only on the amount of turn between the arms, not on their length. To reduce the angle, bring the arms closer together (turn one arm).
steps: Cutting shortens the arms but the opening stays the same.
To reduce the angle, rotate one arm closer to the other.
figure: Three-panel comic: 'Challenge: Reduce this angle.' / 'Angle reduced.' (scissors snipping the arms) / 'The angle is still the same!'
note: The conclusion that the angle is unchanged is printed in the comic; the explanation is mine (consistent with the teacher's note on page 25).

book_label: 2.8 Special Types of Angles, straight angle AOB, page 16 (Math Talk)
question: Is it possible to draw OC such that the two angles (∠AOC and ∠COB, with ∠AOB a straight angle) are equal to each other in size?
answer: Yes. When OA and OB overlap on folding Vidya's notebook, the crease OC divides ∠AOB into two equal-sized angles.
steps: Fold so that OB lies on OA.
The crease through O is OC.
It divides the straight angle into two equal angles.
figure: Straight line A-O-B; ray OC going up-right; second picture shows ∠COB moved so it can be compared with ∠AOC.
note: Solution page 28.

question: Take a rectangular piece of paper and on one of its sides, mark the straight angle AOB. By folding, try to get a line (crease) passing through O that divides ∠AOB into two equal angles. How can it be done?
answer: Fold the paper so that OB overlaps with OA; the crease through O divides the straight angle into two equal angles.
steps: Mark A, O, B on one edge.
Fold so OB falls on OA.
Unfold: the crease through O gives two equal angles.
figure: Three pictures: rectangle with A, O, B on the bottom edge; paper folded; unfolded paper with a vertical crease through O.
note: The fold method is printed in the next sentence of the book.

question: Justify why the two angles are equal. Is there a way to superimpose and check? Can this superimposition be done by folding?
answer: Because OB was folded onto OA, the two arms overlap exactly, so the two angles fit exactly on each other and are equal. Yes, folding itself is the superimposition: fold along the crease and the two angles coincide.
steps: Fold along crease OC.
OA and OB coincide, so ∠AOC fits on ∠COB.
So they are equal.
note: Reasoning computed; the book gives no printed solution.

book_label: 2.8 Special Types of Angles, page 17 (sunburst question)
question: If a straight angle is formed by half of a full turn, how much of a full turn will form a right angle?
answer: 1/4 of a full turn (a quarter turn).
steps: A right angle is half of a straight angle.
Half of half a turn = 1/4 of a full turn.
note: Solution page 29.

question: How many right angles do the windows of your classroom contain? Do you see other right angles in your classroom?
answer: Depends on the classroom (each rectangular window pane has 4 right angles per pane; doors, desks, board corners, book corners are other right angles).
steps: Count panes and corners of the window: 4 right angles per rectangular pane.
Look for corners of the board, door, desks, books.
note: No printed solution for this item (the solutions skip Q1 to Q3 of this box).

question: Join A to other grid points in the figure by a straight line to get a straight angle. What are all the different ways of doing it? (Two dot grids of 7 columns by 6 rows. Left grid: A at row 3, column 4 and B at row 3, column 7 joined by a horizontal segment. Right grid: A at row 3, column 3 and B at row 5, column 5, joined by a diagonal segment through the dot at row 4, column 4.)

parts.label: left grid
parts.question: Join A so that AB makes a straight angle
parts.answer: 3 ways: join A to the three dots to its left on the same row (columns 3, 2, 1).

parts.label: right grid
parts.question: Join A so that AB makes a straight angle
parts.answer: 2 ways: join A to the dots up-left on the same diagonal (row 2, column 2 and row 1, column 1).

answer: Left grid 3 ways, right grid 2 ways: the new segment must lie on the same line as AB, on the opposite side of A.
steps: A straight angle needs the new arm in the exact opposite direction from AB.
Left: AB goes right, so the new arm goes left: 3 dots (columns 1, 2, 3).
Right: AB goes down-right, so the new arm goes up-left: 2 dots.

(Same two grids as Q2.)

parts.question: Join A to grid points so that the new segment is at right angles to AB
parts.answer: 5 ways: the 2 dots above A and the 3 dots below A in column 4.

parts.answer: 4 ways: 2 dots on one side (row 2, column 4 and row 1, column 5) and 2 dots on the other (row 4, column 2 and row 5, column 1).

answer: Left grid 5 ways, right grid 4 ways (the perpendicular to AB through A, taking every grid dot on it).

Right: AB moves 1 right and 1 down per step, so the perpendicular moves 1 right and 1 up (or 1 left and 1 down): dots (row 2, col 4), (row 1, col 5), (row 4, col 2), (row 5, col 1).

question: Get a slanting crease on the paper. Now, try to get another crease that is perpendicular to the slanting crease. a. How many right angles do you have now? Justify why the angles are exact right angles. b. Describe how you folded the paper so that any other person who doesn't know the process can simply follow your description to get the right angle.

parts.label: a
parts.question: How many right angles? Justify.
parts.answer: Four right angles. Each angle is 1/4 of the complete angle.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Describe how you folded the paper.
parts.answer: Explore different ways of doing it (open-ended).

answer: a) Four right angles, each 1/4 of a full turn. b) Open-ended; explore different ways.
steps: Fold the slanting crease line onto itself (so the two halves of the crease coincide) to make the perpendicular crease through a point on it.
Four equal angles form around the point, each a quarter of a full turn.
note: Solution page 'Page No. 29'. The folding step in 'steps' is my suggestion (computed); the book only says explore different ways.

question: Angles are classified in three groups as shown (a box with three columns of angle drawings). Right angles are shown in the second group. What could be the common feature of the other two groups?
answer: First group: all angles are less than a right angle (less than a quarter turn), called acute angles. Third group: all angles are greater than a right angle but less than a straight angle (more than a quarter turn, less than a half turn), called obtuse angles.
steps: Compare each group's angles with an L-shaped right angle.
Left group is smaller than a right angle; right group is bigger but under a straight angle.
figure: Box with three columns of drawn angles: narrow angles (left), L-shaped right angles (middle), wide angles (right).
note: The book states the answer in the following text lines.

question: Identify acute, right, obtuse and straight angles in the previous figures.
answer: In the classification box: left group acute, middle group right, right group obtuse. Straight angles appear in Fig. 2.11 (angle AOB) and the folded-paper figures (angle AOB with O on the line).
steps: Classify angles by comparing with a right angle.
A straight angle has arms in a line.
figure: The classification box and earlier figures of this chapter.
note: No printed solution for this item; 'previous figures' is ambiguous (could include all earlier figures). The answer here is my reading.

question: Make a few acute angles and a few obtuse angles. Draw them in different orientations.
answer: Draw angles smaller than a right angle (acute) and angles between a right angle and a straight angle (obtuse), turned in different directions. The book shows five acute and four obtuse sample drawings.
steps: Acute: less than a quarter turn.
Obtuse: more than a quarter turn but less than a half turn.
Rotate the drawings to different orientations.
figure: Solution page: five acute angles and four obtuse angles drawn in different orientations.
note: Solution gives sample drawings only (open-ended).

question: Do you know what the words acute and obtuse mean? Acute means sharp and obtuse means blunt. Why do you think these words have been chosen?
answer: In acute angles the opening of the edges is less than in obtuse angles, which have larger openings: acute angles look sharp (pointed), obtuse angles look blunt (wide).
steps: A small opening makes a sharp point.
A large opening makes a blunt shape.

question: Find out the number of acute angles in each of the figures below. What will be the next figure and how many acute angles will it have? Do you notice any pattern in the numbers? (Figures: (i) one triangle; (ii) the triangle divided into 4 small triangles; (iii) divided into 7 small triangles.)

parts.label: i
parts.question: Acute angles in the first figure

parts.label: ii
parts.question: Acute angles in the second figure

parts.label: iii
parts.question: Acute angles in the third figure

answer: 3, 12, 21; the next figure has 30 acute angles. The numbers increase by 9; the number of small triangles is 1, 4, 7, 10 and each has 3 acute angles. (The book says the pattern is 3 × 0 + 1, 3 × 1 + 1, 3 × 2 + 1, 3 × 3 + 1,... where 0, 1, 2, 3, ... are the numbers of inner triangles.)
steps: All the small triangles are equilateral, so each has 3 acute angles.
Number of triangles: 1, 4, 7, 10 gives 3, 12, 21, 30 acute angles.
figure: Three figures: one triangle; a triangle split into 4 by joining midpoints; the split into 7 small triangles (top, left, right and middle triangles further divided).
note: The printed pattern '3 × 0 + 1, 3 × 1 + 1, ...' counts the triangles (1, 4, 7, 10), which are then each multiplied by 3 acute angles; as printed it is not literally 3, 12, 21, 30. 'The next figure' is the one with one more level of triangles (10 small triangles).

question: What is the measure of a straight angle in degrees? What is the measure of a right angle in degrees?
answer: Straight angle = 180 degrees; right angle = 90 degrees.
steps: A full turn is 360 degrees; a straight angle is half a full turn, so 180 degrees
Two right angles form a straight angle, so a right angle is 180 / 2 = 90 degrees
figure: Line AOB with O between A and B and a 180 units fan above it; right angle AOB with a 90 units fan
note: The book text answers it right after the question (printed in the text, not on the solutions pages).

steps: Each angle = 360 / number of parts

Follow-up: Making use of the medium sized and large sized marks, is it possible to count the number of units in 5s or 10s?)

question: Will these (the numbers written on the protractor) make it easier to read the angles? There are two sets of numbers on the protractor: one increasing from right to left and the other increasing from left to right. Why does it include two sets of numbers?
answer: Open-ended. The two scales let you read from either arm as the 0 line (base arm on the right or on the left).
steps: One scale starts at 0 on the right and increases anticlockwise
The other starts at 0 on the left and increases clockwise
Use the scale whose 0 lies on the arm you chose as the base

question: Did you include angles such as ∠TOQ? Which set of markings did you use, inner or outer? What is the measure of ∠TOS?
answer: ∠TOQ = 125° (same as ∠QOT). ∠TOS = 35° (same as ∠SOT). Either scale works if it is read from the same 0 arm.

∠TOS = ∠SOT = 35°

question: Can you use the numbers marked to find the angle without counting the number of markings? Here, OT and OS pass through the numbers 20 and 55 on the outer scale. How many units of 1 degree are contained between these two arms? Can subtraction be used here?
answer: Yes. 55 − 20 = 35 units, so the angle between OT and OS is 35°. Yes, subtraction can be used.
steps: Read both arms on the same (outer) scale: 20 and 55
Subtract: 55 − 20 = 35 degrees
figure: Same protractor with OT through outer 20 and OS through outer 55

question: Make your own protractor by paper folding. 1. Draw a circle of a convenient radius on a sheet of paper. Cut out the circle (Fig. 2.13). A circle or one full turn is 360°. 2. Fold the circle to get two equal halves and cut it through the crease to get a semicircle. Write '0°' in the bottom right corner of the semicircle. 3. Fold the semi-circular sheet in half as shown in Fig. 2.15 to form a quarter circle. 4. Fold the sheet again as shown in Figs. 2.16 and 2.17. 5. Continue with another half fold as shown in Fig. 2.18. 6. Unfold and mark the creases as OB, OC, ..., etc., as shown in Fig. 2.19 and Fig. 2.20.
answer: Open-ended craft. Resulting marks on the semicircle: 0°, 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 90°, 112.5°, 135°, 157.5°, 180°.
steps: Circle = 360°; half fold gives 180° (write 180° at left bottom corner)
Quarter circle gives 90° (mark at top)
Next fold gives 45° and 135°
figure: Fig. 2.13 circle folded to a semicircle; Fig. 2.14 semicircle with 180 and 0 corners and a 180 units fan; Fig. 2.15 quarter fold with 90 at the top; Figs 2.16 and 2.17 show the 45 and 135 creases; Fig. 2.18 another half fold; Fig. 2.19 semicircle with points A (right end), B, C, D, E (top), F, G, H, I (left end), centre O; Fig. 2.20 same with 0, 22.5, 45, 67.5, 90, 112.5, 135, 157.5, 180

question: In Fig. 2.19, we have ∠AOB = ∠BOC = ∠COD = ∠DOE = ∠EOF = ∠FOG = ∠GOH = ∠HOI = _____. Why?
answer: 22.5°. The straight angle of 180° is divided into eight equal parts, so each angle = 180°/8 = 22.5°.

note: The solutions page cites Fig. 2.20 and the odd phrase 'each of the right angles'; the value 22.5° is clear.

book_label: Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q1
question: Angles in a clock: a. The hands of a clock make different angles at different times. At 1 o'clock, the angle between the hands is 30°. Why? b. What will be the angle at 2 o'clock? And at 4 o'clock? 6 o'clock? c. Explore other angles made by the hands of a clock.

parts.label: a
parts.question: At 1 o'clock the angle between the hands is 30°. Why?

parts.label: c
parts.question: Explore other angles made by the hands of a clock

answer: a. The clock's 360° is divided into 12 equal parts, so the angle between two successive numbers is 360/12 = 30°. b. 2 o'clock = 60°, 4 o'clock = 120°, 6 o'clock = 180°. c. e.g. 3 o'clock = 90°, 9 o'clock = 270°.

question: The angle of a door: Is it possible to express the amount by which a door is opened using an angle? What will be the vertex of the angle and what will be the arms of the angle?

Keeping one arm, say IN, as the reference (base), the other arm IT should take a turn of 30°. Step 1: We begin with the base and draw ray IN. Step 2: We will place the centre point of the protractor on I and align IN to the 0 line. Step 3: Now, starting from 0, count your degrees (0, 10, 30) up to 30 on the protractor. Mark point T at the label 30°. Step 4: Using a ruler join the point I and T. ∠TIN = 30° is the required angle.

Count up to 30 and mark point T
Join I and T with a ruler; ∠TIN = 30°

question: Angle guessing game with two teams. Team 1 secretly chooses an angle measure, for example 49°, and makes an angle with that measure using a protractor without Team 2 being able to see it. Team 2 now gets to look at the angle. They have to quickly discuss and guess the number of degrees in the angle (without using a protractor!). Team 1 now demonstrates the true measure of the angle with a protractor. Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between their guess and the correct measure. For example, if Team 2 guesses 39°, then they score 10 points (49°−39°). Each team gets five turns. The winner is the team with the lowest score.
answer: Open-ended game.
steps: Team 1 makes a secret angle
Team 2 guesses
Score = absolute difference between guess and true measure
Five turns each; lowest score wins

question: Same two teams, new rules. Team 1 announces to all an angle measure, e.g., 34°. A player from Team 2 must draw that angle on the board without using a protractor. Other members of Team 2 can help the player by speaking words like 'Make it bigger!' or 'Make it smaller!'. A player from Team 1 measures the angle with a protractor for all to see. Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between Team 2's angle size and the intended angle size. For example, if the player's angle from Team 2 is measured to be 25°, then Team 2 scores 9 points (34°−25°). Each team gets five turns. The winner is again the team with the lowest score.
answer: Open-ended game.
steps: Team 1 announces a measure
Team 2 draws without a protractor
Team 1 measures
Score = absolute difference; lowest total wins

question: Puzzle: I am an acute angle. If you double my measure, you get an acute angle. If you triple my measure, you will get an acute angle again. If you quadruple (four times) my measure, you will get an acute angle yet again! But if you multiply my measure by 5, you will get an obtuse angle measure. What are the possibilities for my measure?
answer: The acute angle can be 19°, 20°, 21° and 22° (whole-number degrees).
steps: 4 × measure < 90, so measure < 22.5
5 × measure > 90, so measure > 18
Whole degrees between 18 and 22.5: 19, 20, 21, 22
note: Solutions list whole numbers only; strictly the range is any angle greater than 18° and less than 22.5°.
